name: Choguita Rarámuri
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: [p. 43] Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral. [p. 134] ... stress is underlyingly present for at least some morphemes in this language, and can create lexical contrasts. ... a. ˈmúri ‘basket’, ‘canasta’ b. muˈrí ‘turtle’, ‘tortuga’ ... the stress system of Choguita Rarámuri is in part phonologically determined and partly morphologically-conditioned, as attested in other lexical stress systems. [p. 135] There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. ... Stress is left-aligned and assigned in the first (2a), second (2b–c) or third (2d–e) syllable of the word. [p. 151] Lexical stress in roots blocks morphologically-conditioned stress shifts; stress in these cases will be fixed on the first, second or third syllable, regardless of what suffixes are attached. ... In words containing unstressed roots and stress-neutral suffix, stress will be assigned by default on the second syllable of the root or the only syllable of monosyllabic roots. ... stress shifts rightward. [p. 407] Given that there is no role for contrastive vowel length in stress assignment, this is a weight-insensitive iambic system.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: cent2131 (Central Tarahumara = Choguita Rarámuri, Guachochi municipality, 'Central' dialect area per Caballero et al. 2022 p. 2) is not in the catalog. All four target items are by Gabriela Caballero and are about word stress in this variety. Read in full: (a) Caballero 2005 ROA-706 manuscript (downloaded from roa.rutgers.edu, 27 pp.): mixed lexical/default stress system, initial trisyllabic window, no secondary stress, default 2nd-syllable stem stress with weak suffixes and 3rd-syllable with strong suffixes (p. 15); (b) Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 OUP chapter (author preprint downloaded from Yuan Chai's github page): stress lexically contrastive, initial three-syllable window, non-iterative (p. 3), chapter otherwise about tone f0/voice quality and intonation; (c) not in the target list but the authoritative source: Caballero 2022 A grammar of Choguita Rarámuri (LangSci Press, open access; copy already held by the project in our check tree), §2.1.2 p. 43 and ch. 5 pp. 133-166. Not obtainable: Caballero 2011 Linguistics (De Gruyter, closed, abstract not retrievable) and Caballero & Carroll 2015 IJAL (closed; abstract saved from Semantic Scholar) — both medium priority only, since the 2022 grammar covers and cites them. The 2008 UC Berkeley dissertation is linked from the author's site only via a login-gated Google Drive link and eScholarship search returned nothing fetchable. Recommended coding for a new catalog record: lexical stress, initial three-syllable window, left-aligned, no secondary stress, deciding source Caballero 2022 grammar p. 43.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs like ˈmúri 'basket' vs muˈrí 'turtle') and is confined to an initial three-syllable window: it falls on the first, second or third syllable of the word, never further right. Roots are either stressed (fixed stress in the 1st or 2nd syllable across paradigms) or unstressed; unstressed roots get default stress on their second syllable (or the only syllable of a monosyllabic root) when combined with stress-neutral suffixes, and stress shifts one syllable rightward onto a stress-shifting suffix (rule (17), p. 151). A three-way lexical tone contrast (HL, L, H) is realized only on the stressed syllable. Acoustic cues are primarily intensity and duration; unstressed vowels reduce/delete (§5.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. That is, there is no impressionistic evidence of rhythmic prominence' (p. 135); the 2022 preprint calls the system non-iterative.
new_statements.exceptions: Stressed roots block morphological stress shifts; stress shift alone can encode imperative, denominalization and applicative categories (chs. 9, 11); the three-syllable window is enforced in compounds and multiply suffixed words, and Spanish loanwords whose source stress lies outside the window are truncated to keep it inside (§7.3); fourth-syllable stress is unattested.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prosodic word), for both bare/citation forms and inflected words; window counted from the left edge of the word. Lexical tone is dependent on stress; the language is described as a stress-accent language with lexical tone (hybrid), not as a tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Choguita Rarámuri (community of Choguita, municipality of Guachochi, Chihuahua). Caballero 2022 §1.1.2.1 (p. 6) places it in Ethnologue's Central Tarahumara [tar] (= Glottolog cent2131), in a transitional area between the Central and Northern dialects of Valiñas' (2001)/INALI classification; Glottolog itself files the grammar under cent2131. Caballero's 2005 ROA paper labels the same data 'Central Raramuri'. Note that Brambila 1953 and Lionnet (Norogachi), also filed under cent2131 by Glottolog, are called a 'Northern variety' by Caballero 2022: 12.

new_statements.reading: Lexical (contrastive) word stress, morphologically conditioned, confined to a left-edge three-syllable window (stress on syllable 1, 2 or 3; never further right). One stress per word, no secondary stress (Caballero 2005 p. 3; Caballero, Chai & Garellek 2022 preprint p. 3). Default for lexically unstressed roots: second syllable of the stem with stress-neutral suffixes, third syllable with stress-shifting suffixes (Caballero 2005 p. 15; grammar Table 2.3 p. 43). Correlates: duration and vowel reduction; a separate three-way lexical tone contrast rides on the stressed syllable. on the catalog's classification this is a lexical system with an initial three-syllable window (not quantity-sensitive; no contrastive vowel length).

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same analysis as the catalog source (Caballero 2022 grammar §2.1.2, ch. 5): lexically contrastive stress inside an initial three-syllable window, stressed/unstressed roots, stress-shifting/stress-neutral suffixes, default second (neutral) or third (shifting) syllable, no secondary stress. The dissertation is the 2008 precursor of the grammar's chapter 5; nothing differs in placement or type. The ELAR collection description itself is silent on stress (it only mentions 'Excel databases of.. prosodic and morphological properties').
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per prosodic word, no secondary stress. Stress is lexical for some roots (minimal pairs by stress position); roots are stressed or unstressed and suffixes stress-shifting or stress-neutral. Words with an unstressed root and no stress-shifting suffix take stress on the second root syllable; with a stress-shifting suffix, on the third syllable of the word; lexical root stress blocks these defaults. Stress never falls to the right of the third syllable (initial three-syllable window, left-aligned). Correlates: vowel duration (stressed roughly twice unstressed), unstressed-vowel reduction/deletion, onset augmentation. Derived vowel length plays no role in stress placement (not weight-sensitive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly none: '(b) There is no secondary stress' (p. 173); 'there is no audible secondary stress' (p. 176).
new_statements.exceptions: Incorporated (body-part incorporation) constructions show a dominant stress pattern deleting inherent stress of the members (p. 174 item i, §4.3.2); imperative final-stem stress shift (§3.4.1.3, §3.5.2.4); in multiply affixed words stress depends on the Stem (root + first suffix) only (item g).

new_statements.translation: [p. viii] ACCENTUATION. For the Tarahumara words in this vocabulary we use the same accentuation rules as in Spanish, so when the stress falls on the penultimate syllable we do not mark it. Some words carry two accents. [p. v] There is also some variation between the vowels i and e when they are not in the stressed syllable, e.g. quima or quema 'blanket'. [p. 135] 2. (The second verb class comprises) those that mark the future by removing the accent from the root and adding the suffix -méa in the singular forms and the third person plural, and -boa or -poa in the first and second person plural.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical, morphologically conditioned stress: stress must be marked per word (not fixed) and a future suffix (-méa) removes root stress, which parallels Caballero's stress-shifting suffixes (Choguita future singular -ma/-méa). The work describes the Samachique (municipio de Guachochi) variety of 'la región tarahumara del centro' = Central Tarahumara [tar], the same Glottolog language as Choguita but a different community; it adds no placement rule, window or default, so it neither refines nor contradicts the Choguita statement. The 'dos acentos' remark is orthographic and is not evidence against Caballero's 'no secondary stress' for Choguita.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary states no placement rule. It treats stress as a property to be written word by word with Spanish orthographic conventions (penultimate stress unmarked, any other position marked with an acute), i.e. stress position is not predictable from the spelling alone and varies across words (entries show e.g. coná 'sal', chomá 'moco', saté 'arena', boní 'hermano menor' with final stress beside unmarked penultimate forms such as ane, cona-hua); stress interacts with morphology: class-2 verbs lose root stress before the stressed future suffix -méa (a stress-shifting suffix), and unstressed i/e neutralize outside the tonic syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the orthographic remark 'Hay algunas palabras que llevan dos acentos' (some words carry two written accents), unexplained; no statement about secondary stress as such.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb class 2 (future in -méa/-boa/-poa with loss of root accent) and a subclass with suppletive plural roots; free variation i~e in unstressed syllables; l~r variation word-medially.

tone_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela & Marc Garellek. 2018. Multidimensional tonal realization and prosodic variation in Choguita Rarámuri (Tarahumara). Poster presented at the 16th Conference on Laboratory Phonology (LabPhon 16), Lisbon, Portugal.
tone_statements.quote: Choguita Rarámuri (Uto-Aztecan; Mexico): • 3 lexical tones (HL, H and L) exclusively realized in stressed syllables • Low pitch target of HL tone may be realized in post-tonic syllable (if any) • Preliminary results show high degree of speaker variability • Interactions between lexical tones and H% at the end of declaratives … • Speakers employ a variety of strategies for achieving a common goal: separation of three tonal categories. • Pitch-independent strategies: longer duration for L tones • Possibly pitch-dependent: creakier voicing for L tones
tone_statements.locator: single-page poster (unpaginated): introduction panel 'Lexical tones in Choguita Raramuri' (bullets) and Conclusions panel
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones, HL (falling), H and L, realized only on the stressed syllable (HL's low target may fall on the post-tonic); acoustic study of 4 speakers: L tones longer and creakier.

tone_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela & Sharon Rose. 2018. Construction-based tone patterns in Choguita Raramuri and Cilungu. Proc. 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 41-45. doi 10.21437/TAL.2018-9. (Author's page lists it as: Caballero, Gabriela. 2018b. Construction-based inflectional tone patterns in Choguita Rarámuri.)
tone_statements.quote: Choguita Rarámuri is a prosodically complex language with both stress-accent and a three-way lexical tonal contrast (with H, L and HL tones). Tone distribution is dependent on stress-accent, which is in turn morphologically governed. As a result, many tonal patterns in this language are predictable based on the lexical tone properties of roots and affixes and the distribution of stress. In addition, tone also serves a morphological role in the language, via patterns of grammatical tone, morphologically conditioned tonal effects and paradigmatic distribution of tonal melodies, all of which may trigger overwriting of lexical tones.
tone_statements.locator: abstract on the ISCA Archive landing page (paper pp. 41-45)

tone_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela (2017). Choguita Rarámuri (Tarahumara) language description and documentation: A guide to the deposited collection and associated materials. Language Documentation and Conservation 11. University of Hawaii Press. pp. 224–255.
tone_statements.quote: CR features a highly complex stress system with elaborate lexical and morphological conditioning governing its distribution and an initial three-syllable stress window … In addition to stress, CR possesses a tone system that contrasts three tones (high, low and falling) in stressed syllables. … This research has so far shown that stress and tone are not only phonologically independent systems in CR, but they are also acoustically distinct: duration and intensity are correlates of stress, whereas fundamental frequency (F0) is the primary correlate of tone (Caballero & Carroll 2015).
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones (high, low, falling) contrasting only in stressed syllables, independent of a lexically/morphologically conditioned stress within an initial three-syllable window.

tone_statements.citation: Garellek, Marc and Aguilar, Andrés and Caballero, Gabriela and Carroll, Lucien (2015). Lexical and post-lexical tone in Choguita Rarámuri. In Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Glasgow, Scotland.
tone_statements.quote: In terms of its word-level prosody, CR has lexical stress with complex morphological conditioning [3, 4], and which is correlated primarily with changes in syllable intensity and duration [5]. In contrast to many other toneless Uto-Aztecan languages, in CR lexically-stressed syllables obligatorily bear one of three lexical tones: low (L), high (H), and falling (HL). Stressless syllables are lexically toneless [5].
tone_statements.locator: paper p. 1 (unpaginated 5-page ICPhS paper), section 1 Introduction
tone_statements.summary: Three lexical tones (high, low, falling) only on the lexically stressed syllable; stressless syllables toneless; separate lexical stress cued by intensity and duration; lead tones, H% intonational.

tone_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela and Carroll, Lucien and Garellek, Marc (2014). Tone-intonation interactions in Choguita Rarámuri (Tarahumara). In Workshop on the Sound Systems of Mexico and Central America, Yale University.
tone_statements.quote: Choguita Rarámuri (CR; Tarahumara), a UA language of northern Mexico, has both stress-accent and tone with complex morphological conditioning. Stress and tone are not only phonologically independent systems, but are also acoustically distinct; duration and intensity are correlates of stress, whereas fundamental frequency (F0) is the primary correlate of tone (Caballero & Carroll 2013). In addition to using F0 to mark lexical and morphological distinctions (a three-way contrast between HL, L and M in stressed syllables), CR exploits F0 intonationally.
tone_statements.summary: Three-way lexical/morphological tone contrast HL, L, M, only on the stressed syllable; word stress is a separate system (duration, intensity). AP-initial M, pitch accents HL*/L*/H*, final H%.

tone_statements.citation: Caballero, Gabriela (2008). Choguita Rarámuri (Tarahumara) phonology and morphology. PhD dissertation, UC Berkeley.
tone_statements.quote: While there is robust evidence that Choguita Rarámuri has a stress system … there is also evidence that in this language tone is part of the lexical realization of at least a few morphemes. So far, I have only been able to identify the tonal minimal pairs listed in (103). In these minimal pairs, there is a contrast between a high tone (marked with an acute accent) and a low tone (marked with a grave accent), where tone is associated with stress (i.e., I have only detected tonal contrasts in stressed syllables).
tone_statements.summary: High vs low tone contrast only on stressed syllables of a few roots (ten minimal pairs; low functional load, tonogenesis in progress); separate lexical stress in an initial three-syllable window.

sources.quote: [p. 43] Stress in Choguita Rarámuri is lexically contrastive and assigned to the first, second or third syllable within an initial three-syllable window. Stress in inflected words is determined by the stress properties of both roots and suffixes: roots are stressed or unstressed (with fixed or shifting stress across paradigms, respectively), while suffixes are stress-shifting or stress-neutral. [p. 135] There is no evidence for secondary stress in Choguita Rarámuri. […] Stress is left-aligned and assigned in the first (2a), second (2b–c) or third (2d–e) syllable of the word.

sources.quote: [p. 173] 1) Choguita Rarámuri stress properties a) Each prosodic word has a single stress. b) There is no secondary stress (i.e. this is an unbounded system). c) Roots can be stressed or unstressed. d) Affixes are either stress-shifting or stress-neutral, ... e) In words containing no stressed roots or stress-shifting suffixes, stress falls in the second syllable of the root. [p. 174] f) In words containing an unstressed root and a stress-shifting suffix, stress falls in the third syllable of the word ... h) Lexical stress in roots blocks morphologically-conditioned second and third syllable stress. ... j) There is an initial three-syllable window.

sources.quote: An important phonological property in Choguita Rarámuri morphology is stress. The general properties of this language's stress system can be summarized as follows: (i) roots are underlyingly stressed or unstressed; (ii) suffixes are either 'stress-shifting' or 'stress-neutral' (occurring within vs. outside of the domain of stress assignment); (iii) stress is in either the verbal root or a stress-shifting suffix (if the root is unstressed); (iv) stress is never beyond the third syllable from left to right; (v) syllables are underlyingly coda-less and post-tonic syncope yields derived consonant clusters; and (vi) consonant clusters often demarcate a boundary between a base and any later, inflectional morphology of the finite verb.

sources.note: Lexical stress: roots underlyingly stressed or unstressed; suffixes split into stress-shifting (Derived Stem, Aspectual Stem, Finite Verb positions) vs stress-neutral classes (scheme (7), p. 170); stress falls on the root or on a stress-shifting suffix when the root is unstressed; stress confined to a three-syllable window from the left edge; imperative stress shift applies within Inner and Derived Stem levels (scheme (6), p. 169); post-tonic vowel deletion/syncope. Foot referred to (Evidential subcategorizes for a foot to its left, p. 185) but foot type (iambic/trochaic) not stated. Secondary

sources.citation: Caballero, Gabriela & Sharon Rose. 2018. Construction-based tone patterns in Choguita Raramuri and Cilungu. Proc. 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 41-45. doi 10.21437/TAL.2018-9. (Author's page lists it as: Caballero, Gabriela. 2018b. Construction-based inflectional tone patterns in Choguita Rarámuri.)
sources.quote: Choguita Rarámuri is a prosodically complex language with both stress-accent and a three-way lexical tonal contrast (with H, L and HL tones). Tone distribution is dependent on stress-accent, which is in turn morphologically governed. As a result, many tonal patterns in this language are predictable based on the lexical tone properties of roots and affixes and the distribution of stress. In addition, tone also serves a morphological role in the language, via patterns of grammatical tone, morphologically conditioned tonal effects and paradigmatic distribution of tonal melodies, all of which may trigger overwriting of lexical tones.
sources.locator: abstract on the ISCA Archive landing page (paper pp. 41-45)
sources.note: Choguita Rarámuri has stress-accent plus a three-way lexical tone contrast (H, L, HL) realized on the stressed syllable; tone distribution depends on morphologically governed stress; tone also has a morphological role (grammatical tone, morphologically conditioned tonal effects, paradigmatic tonal melodies) that can overwrite lexical tone; argues for a construction-based analysis of inflectional tone.

tone.quote: This chapter addresses the challenges of characterizing the tonal system of Choguita Rarámuri (CR) (Uto-Aztecan; Mexico) within the context of a documentation-based reference grammar of the language. This chapter discusses: (i) the role that tone serves in the morphological organization of CR; (ii) challenges of characterizing this system within the context of a reference grammar; and (iii) how synchronic variation in tonal realization is incorporated in the grammatical description of CR and its implications for assessing change in progress in the language.

sources.quote: we propose that (i) stress-accent and tone are phonologically distinct systems in Choguita Rarámuri; (ii) stress-accent and tone are independent in terms of their acoustic encoding; (iii) both stress-accent and tone are governed in their distribution and makeup by lexical and morphological conditions; (iv) the tone system features a three-way contrast between HL, L, and M; and (v) lexical tonal contrasts are exclusively realized in stressed syllables—that is, tonal distribution is dependent on stress-accent.
sources.note: Acoustic study establishing stress (intensity/duration) as independent of tone; needed for the phonetic-correlates entry.

tone.says: From the Crossref/OpenAlex record and the two open companion pieces that cite it (SSMCA 2014 abstract as 'Caballero & Carroll 2013'; Garellek et al. 2015 ICPhS ref [5]): instrumental study of Choguita Raramuri word prosody showing stress and tone are independent systems, stress cued by duration/intensity and tone by F0, with a three-way lexical tonal contrast confined to stressed syllables (labelled HL/L/M in the 2014 abstract, HL/H/L in the 2015 ICPhS paper; stressless syllables toneless).

tone.quote: While there is robust evidence that Choguita Rarámuri has a stress system … there is also evidence that in this language tone is part of the lexical realization of at least a few morphemes. So far, I have only been able to identify the tonal minimal pairs listed in (103). In these minimal pairs, there is a contrast between a high tone (marked with an acute accent) and a low tone (marked with a grave accent), where tone is associated with stress (i.e., I have only detected tonal contrasts in stressed syllables).
tone.summary: High vs low tone contrast only on stressed syllables of a few roots (ten minimal pairs; low functional load, tonogenesis in progress); separate lexical stress in an initial three-syllable window.

tone.quote: CR features a highly complex stress system with elaborate lexical and morphological conditioning governing its distribution and an initial three-syllable stress window … In addition to stress, CR possesses a tone system that contrasts three tones (high, low and falling) in stressed syllables. … This research has so far shown that stress and tone are not only phonologically independent systems in CR, but they are also acoustically distinct: duration and intensity are correlates of stress, whereas fundamental frequency (F0) is the primary correlate of tone (Caballero & Carroll 2015).
tone.summary: Three lexical tones (high, low, falling) contrasting only in stressed syllables, independent of a lexically/morphologically conditioned stress within an initial three-syllable window.

tone.quote: In terms of its word-level prosody, CR has lexical stress with complex morphological conditioning [3, 4], and which is correlated primarily with changes in syllable intensity and duration [5]. In contrast to many other toneless Uto-Aztecan languages, in CR lexically-stressed syllables obligatorily bear one of three lexical tones: low (L), high (H), and falling (HL). Stressless syllables are lexically toneless [5].
tone.locator: paper p. 1 (unpaginated 5-page ICPhS paper), section 1 Introduction
tone.summary: Three lexical tones (high, low, falling) only on the lexically stressed syllable; stressless syllables toneless; separate lexical stress cued by intensity and duration; lead tones, H% intonational.
tone.says: Three lexical tones (high, low, falling) only on the lexically stressed syllable; stressless syllables toneless; separate lexical stress cued by intensity and duration; lead tones, H% intonational.

tone.quote: Choguita Rarámuri (CR; Tarahumara), a UA language of northern Mexico, has both stress-accent and tone with complex morphological conditioning. Stress and tone are not only phonologically independent systems, but are also acoustically distinct; duration and intensity are correlates of stress, whereas fundamental frequency (F0) is the primary correlate of tone (Caballero & Carroll 2013). In addition to using F0 to mark lexical and morphological distinctions (a three-way contrast between HL, L and M in stressed syllables), CR exploits F0 intonationally.
tone.summary: Three-way lexical/morphological tone contrast HL, L, M, only on the stressed syllable; word stress is a separate system (duration, intensity). AP-initial M, pitch accents HL*/L*/H*, final H%.
tone.says: Three-way lexical/morphological tone contrast HL, L, M, only on the stressed syllable; word stress is a separate system (duration, intensity). AP-initial M, pitch accents HL*/L*/H*, final H%.
